items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's prove the following proposition using the contrapositive:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is odd}}_{P(n)}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{n \text{ is odd}}_{Q(n)}]

Content:
To prove [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q,] it suffices to prove the contrapositive [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.] So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

Content:
> The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:
> [MATH: \underbrace{ n \text{ is even}}_{\lnot Q(n)}
> \quad\Rightarrow\quad
> \underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is even}}_{\lnot P(n)}]
> We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

Content:
We start by using the fact that [MATH: n] is even.

Content:
> If [MATH: n] is even, then [MATH: n=2a] for some integer [MATH: a.]

Content:
The idea is to substitute [MATH: n=2a] into the expression [MATH: 3n+2] and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
> Therefore,
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 3(2a) + 2; = 6a + 2; = 2(3a + 1)_(⏟)_(b).]

Content:
Now, if we define another integer [MATH: b=3a+1] (highlighted above), we have that [MATH: 3n+2 = 2b,] which shows that [MATH: 3n+2] is indeed a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
> Let [MATH: b=3a+1.] Since [MATH: a] is an integer, we have that [MATH: b] is an integer.
>
> Hence, we have
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 2(3a + 1)_(⏟)_(b); = 2b,]
> which is a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
Finally, we write our conclusion.

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: 3n+2] is even.

Content:
Now that we've figured out the details, let's state the full proof.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
One type of indirect proof is the so-called proof by contrapositive. The method is based on the fact that the implication
[MATH: P \Rightarrow Q]
is logically equivalent to its contrapositive
[MATH: \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P.]
So, instead of proving the statement directly, we can instead prove its contrapositive form.

Content:
The outline of a typical contrapositive proof is the following:

Content:
> Statement. If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q.]
>
> Proof.
>
> > Since [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P,] we'll prove the contrapositive [MATH: \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P.]
> >
> > Assumption: Suppose [MATH: \lnot Q.]
> >
> > Explanation of what [MATH: \lnot Q] means using axioms, definitions, or other results.
> >
> > Algebraic techniques, logic, and further definitions or axioms are used to demonstrate, through a series of inferences, that [MATH: \lnot Q] implies [MATH: \lnot P.]
> >
> > Conclusion: Therefore, [MATH: \lnot P.] So, since [MATH: \lnot Q\Rightarrow \lnot P,] by the contrapositive [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q.]

Content:
In many cases, proving the contrapositive form of a statement is easier than proving the original statement. In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove parity statements using the contrapositive.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Proving Parity Statements by Contrapositive

Content:
Let's prove the following proposition using the contrapositive:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is odd}}_{P(n)}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{n \text{ is odd}}_{Q(n)}]

Content:
To prove [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q,] it suffices to prove the contrapositive [MATH: \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P.] So, let's write down the contrapositive of our statement.

Content:
> The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:
> [MATH: \underbrace{ n \text{ is even}}_{\lnot Q(n)}
> \quad\Rightarrow\quad
> \underbrace{3n+2 \text{ is even}}_{\lnot P(n)}]
> We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

Content:
We start by using the fact that [MATH: n] is even.

Content:
> If [MATH: n] is even, then [MATH: n=2a] for some integer [MATH: a.]

Content:
The idea is to substitute [MATH: n=2a] into the expression [MATH: 3n+2] and show it is even by writing it as a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
> Therefore,
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 3(2a) + 2; = 6a + 2; = 2(3a + 1)_(⏟)_(b).]

Content:
Now, if we define another integer [MATH: b=3a+1] (highlighted above), we have that [MATH: 3n+2 = 2b,] which shows that [MATH: 3n+2] is indeed a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
> Let [MATH: b=3a+1.] Since [MATH: a] is an integer, we have that [MATH: b] is an integer.
>
> Hence, we have
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 2(3a + 1)_(⏟)_(b); = 2b,]
> which is a multiple of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
Finally, we write our conclusion.

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: 3n+2] is even.

Content:
Now that we've figured out the details, let's state the full proof.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Stating the Full Proof

Content:
Proposition:

Content:
[MATH: 3n+2 \text{ is odd}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
n \text{ is odd}]

Content:
Proof:

Content:
> The contrapositive form of the given statement is as follows:
> [MATH: n \text{ is even}
> \quad\Rightarrow\quad
> 3n+2 \text{ is even}]
> If [MATH: n] is even, then [MATH: n=2a] for some integer [MATH: a.] Therefore,
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 6a + 2; = 2(3a + 1).]
>
> Let [MATH: b=3a+1.] Since [MATH: a] is an integer, we have that [MATH: b] is an integer.
>
> Hence, we have
> [MATH: 3n + 2|= 2(3a + 1); = 2b,]
> which is a multiple of [MATH: 2.]
>
> Therefore, [MATH: 3n+2] is even.
